response:
A content delivery network solves a simple problem: a single origin server, the original computer storing a website's files, sits in one place, but people asking for that website are scattered everywhere. If every request had to travel to that one distant machine, pages would load slowly for anyone far away. So copies of the site's files get stored on many servers around the world, called edge locations, positioned close to where people actually are. When someone visits a website, the request goes to the nearest edge location instead of the far-off origin. If that location already has a saved copy of what's needed, that's called a cache hit, and the content gets delivered almost instantly, without ever bothering the origin server. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries stocking popular books instead of everyone trekking to one national archive; most people find what they need nearby, and only rare requests go to the archive itself. This setup reduces waiting time, spreads out traffic so no single server gets overwhelmed, and keeps things running even if one location has trouble. It's the quiet infrastructure behind fast-loading videos, images, and web pages worldwide.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer where a website's real files live | Everything ultimately traces back here if copies aren't available |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding copies of website content | Keeps delivery fast by shortening the distance data travels |
| Cache hit | When a nearby server already has the requested file | Means near-instant loading without contacting the origin |
| Latency | The delay between asking for something and receiving it | Lower delay makes browsing feel smooth and responsive |
